verdict.text: Verdict: The Phone (3) is a flagship only in Nothing's With the Phone (3), Nothing remains true to its philosophy of developing smartphones that are a little different from the competition. This is evident in the transparent back, the asymmetrical arrangement of the cameras, the slim and fast Nothing OS 3.5, and extras such as the Glyph Matrix with its 486 LEDs. With five years of OS updates and software support until 2032, the Nothing Phone (3) provides further reasons for consideration. Other plus points include the bright AMOLED screen, the good camera system, and the large and fast-charging battery, which should last a whole day of intensive use. That being said, the Nothing Phone (3) also has some minor weaknesses. The Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 is fast but doesn't quite match the €799 asking price purchase price for the base variant. Additionally, you don't get an LTPO AMOLED but only an LPTS display. Nothing also cuts corners on the display glass. While many similarly priced smartphones rely on Gorilla Glass Victus, the Nothing Phone (3) only features the less resistant Gorilla Glass 7i.

paragraphs:
The Nothing Phone (3) is a real flagship smartphone, claims the company. What is certain is that it outshines all previous Nothing phones in terms of performance, battery size, and software support.

However, our review also shows that Nothing has scaled back the hardware ingredients just enough in some areas so that there is no noticeable disadvantage for users.

The Nothing Phone (3), therefore, feels like a high-end smartphone, without actually being one.

With its 1.86 mm thin display frame, the Nothing Phone (3), which is available in black and white, makes a high-quality visual impression. There is also nothing to complain about in terms of workmanship. However, the phone does make a subtle crackling noise when twisted.

The biggest innovation compared to its predecessor is on the transparent back. The iconic Nothing design is still there, but the Glyph interface has been replaced by the Glyph Matrix — a small monochrome display with 489 LEDs.

The Glyph Matrix is located in the top right-hand corner and shows, for example, the battery level or provides information about incoming messages. The displays (aka Glyph Toys) can be switched via a white button underneath. The red LED signals ongoing audio and video recordings by flashing.

The Nothing Phone (3) offers NFC, Bluetooth 6.0, and Wi-Fi 7. Two nano SIMs fit into the SIM slot. An eSIM can also be used instead of the second physical SIM.

The USB-C port only works at USB 2.0 speeds and achieves 36.7 MB/s in the copy test with the Samsung PSSD T7.

The Nothing Phone (3) runs Nothing OS 3.5, which is based on Android 15. Nothing promises five years of OS upgrades up to Android 20. Android security updates will be available every 2 months for seven years.

Nothing OS 3.5 extends the standard Android interface with an independent design and the Essential Space — an AI hub that helps users with everyday tasks.

Essential Space receives its input from the user. If you press the Essential button, it takes a screenshot or takes the image from the camera app along with an optional note. The button can also be used to start audio recordings.

Captured information is automatically transcribed and added to the AI hub. This can be called up and browsed by pressing the button twice.

With the Glyph Matrix, users do not have to make do with the ready-made Glyph Toys. Interested users can join the

The frame, buttons, and SIM tray are made from 100% recycled aluminum. The product packaging is plastic-free and consists of 30% recycled paper fibers.

Nothing does not offer spare parts or repair manuals. However, the smartphone can be sent directly to the manufacturer for repair.

In addition to strong cellular frequency coverage, the Nothing Phone (3) scores with fast and stable Wi-Fi 7.

We measured transfer rates of up to 1,856 Mbps in combination with our reference Asus ROG Rapture GT-AXE11000 reference router.

The Nothing Phone (3) is well suited for navigation. In the test, it guided us almost as precisely to our destination on a 10 km cycle route as the Garmin Venu 2 fitness smartwatch.

The Nothing Phone (3) supports VoLTE and Wi-Fi calls. It delivers good voice quality during calls and also suppresses ambient noise efficiently.

The main, ultra-wide-angle, and telephoto cameras of the Nothing Phone (3) each have a resolution of 50 MP.

In daylight, the main camera equipped with a fast 1/1.3-inch sensor takes beautiful photos that impress with their high dynamic range and realistic colors but sometimes appear blurred. In low light, the large sensor manages to capture many details.

The ultra-wide-angle camera does a good job, but its photos are quite washed out at the edges. The telephoto camera also takes on the task of a macro lens and achieves good image quality if you limit yourself to the 3x optical zoom. The digital zoom works up to 60x, but subjects already become blurred at 5x magnification.

The scope of delivery includes a USB-C cable, a SIM eject tool, and a booklet with safety instructions. A protective film is applied to the display at the factory. Nothing does not offer a 65 W power adapter in its online store.

, and the high touch sampling rate of the responsive AMOLED screen, the Nothing Phone (3) is very smooth to use. The linear vibration motor fits in well with this, as it provides precise haptic feedback.

The optical fingerprint sensor under the display unlocks the smartphone without any noticeable delay. The smartphone can also be unlocked using 2D Face Unlock, which also works reliably, but is much less secure.

The AMOLED screen can get very bright but does not reach the peak brightness of 4,500 cd/m² promised by Nothing for a long time in the test.

With a pure white background, the display has an average brightness of 1,535 cd/m². The brightness values are roughly the same in small picture areas (1,517 cd/m²) and in HDR mode (1,475 cd/m²).

The screen accommodates sensitive users with a fairly high PWM dimming frequency of 1,086 Hz (manufacturer's specification 960 Hz), which is also characterized by a low amplitude.

To dim the screen, some notebooks will simply cycle the backlight on and off in rapid succession - a method called Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) . This cycling frequency should ideally be undetectable to the human eye. If said frequency is too low, users with sensitive eyes may experience strain or headaches or even notice the flickering altogether.

The display backlight flickers at 90 Hz (worst case, e.g., utilizing PWM) .

The frequency of 90 Hz is very low, so the flickering may cause eyestrain and headaches after extended use.

In comparison: 52 % of all tested devices do not use PWM to dim the display. If PWM was detected, an average of 7892 (minimum: 5 - maximum: 343500) Hz was measured.

Measurement series with fixed zoom level and different brightness settings (The amplitude curve at minimum brightness looks flat, but this is due to the scaling. The info box shows the enlarged version of the amplitude at minimum brightness)

The AMOLED panel's color profiles are well tuned. We found the colors to be most accurate in the Standard color mode (the default setting is Vivid).

The screen shows very fast response rates in our tests and should be very well suited for fast-paced gaming.

In comparison, all tested devices range from 0.1 (minimum) to 240 (maximum) ms. » 5 % of all devices are better.

This means that the measured response time is better than the average of all tested devices (20 ms).

In comparison, all tested devices range from 0.165 (minimum) to 636 (maximum) ms. » 20 % of all devices are better.

This means that the measured response time is better than the average of all tested devices (31.2 ms).

The Nothing Phone (3) performs well outdoors. Its fast-responding brightness sensor can increase the brightness of the viewing-angle-stable screen to such an extent that it is easy to read even on sunny days. If the brightness sensor is deactivated, the maximum brightness drops to 774 cd/m².

The Nothing Phone (3) therefore has more than enough power for all everyday tasks and, supported by 12 GB or 16 GB of RAM, is not slowed down by many apps being opened at the same time.

The Nothing Phone (3) can get very warm under load. In the stress test with Burnout Benchmark, we measured surface temperatures of up to 52.1 °C. You won't want to touch the smartphone under this kind of load.

The 3DMark stress tests show that the smartphone quickly throttles the SoC performance under load — to less than 60% of the initial performance in the worst case.

External audio devices can be connected to the smartphone via USB-C and Bluetooth 6.0.

The fairly energy efficient Nothing Phone (3) can be charged with up to 65 W speeds.

According to Nothing, a charging cycle takes 54 minutes — we measured a time of 55 minutes with the 65 W Ugreen 2C1A power supply unit. The battery is already 80% charged after 34 minutes.

The Nothing Phone (3)'s 5,150 mAh cell is the largest battery in a Nothing Phone to date and also clearly outperforms its predecessor in terms of capacity.

The test candidate is also ahead in terms of battery life. With a runtime of nearly 18.5 hours in the WLAN test, it leaves the

The Nothing Phone (3) combines an unusual design with powerful hardware, good cameras, a large battery, and updates until 2032.

However, this high-quality 6.67-inch phone is not exactly a flagship smartphone as advertised by Nothing.
